parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the factor theorem to show that \((x - 3)\) is a factor of \(p(x)\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence write \(p(x)\) as a product of three linear factors.

idea: The factor theorem: \((x - a)\) is a factor of \(p(x)\) exactly when \(p(a) = 0\). Once one factor is known, divide it out (or compare coefficients) to leave a quadratic.

solution.label: b
steps: \(p(x) = (x - 3)\left(x^2 + bx + c\right)\). Compare the \(x^2\) terms: \(b - 3 = -2\), so \(b = 1\). Constant: \(-3c = 6\), so \(c = -2\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the remainder when \(q(x)\) is divided by \((x + 2)\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the remainder when \(q(x)\) is divided by \((2x - 1)\).

idea: The remainder theorem: the remainder when \(q(x)\) is divided by \((ax - b)\) is \(q\left(\frac{b}{a}\right)\), the value of \(q\) where the divisor is zero.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the quotient and the remainder when \(f(x)\) is divided by \(g(x)\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence write \(\dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}\) in the form \(Q(x) + \dfrac{ax + b}{x^2 - x + 2}\).

idea: Polynomial long division: divide the leading term, multiply back, subtract, and repeat until the remainder has lower degree than the divisor. Then \(f = gQ + R\), so \(\frac{f}{g} = Q + \frac{R}{g}\).

stem: The graph of the cubic function \(y = p(x)\) touches the \(x\)-axis at \((2, 0)\), crosses the \(x\)-axis at \((-1, 0)\), and crosses the \(y\)-axis at \((0, 8)\). The graph has a local maximum at \((0, 8)\) and a local minimum at \((2, 0)\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that \(p(x) = 2x^3 - 6x^2 + 8\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Solve the equation \(p(x) = 5\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the set of values of \(k\) for which the equation \(p(x) = k\) has three distinct real solutions.

idea: A root where the graph touches the axis is a repeated root, so it gives a squared factor. A horizontal line \(y = k\) meets a cubic three times exactly when it lies strictly between the local minimum and the local maximum values.

solution.label: a
steps: Touching at \(x = 2\) gives the factor \((x - 2)^2\); crossing at \(x = -1\) gives \((x + 1)\). So \(p(x) = a(x + 1)(x - 2)^2\).

solution.label: c
steps: The local maximum value is 8 and the local minimum value is 0. A horizontal line meets the graph three times exactly when it lies strictly between them.

stem: When the polynomial \(p(x)\) is divided by \((x - 2)\) the remainder is 5, and when it is divided by \((x + 1)\) the remainder is \(-4\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the remainder when \(p(x)\) is divided by \((x - 2)(x + 1)\) can be written as \(ax + b\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the remainder when \(p(x)\) is divided by \((x - 2)(x + 1)\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Given also that \(p(x)\) is a cubic with leading coefficient 1 and that \(p(0) = 3\), find \(p(x)\).

idea: Write \(p(x) = (x - 2)(x + 1)Q(x) + ax + b\). Substituting the zeros of the divisor makes the first term vanish, leaving equations for \(a\) and \(b\).

solution.label: a
steps: The remainder always has lower degree than the divisor. The divisor has degree 2, so the remainder has degree at most 1.

solution.label: c
steps: Leading coefficient 1 and degree 3 mean \(Q(x) = x + c\): \(p(x) = (x - 2)(x + 1)(x + c) + 3x - 1\).

stem: This question is about the polynomial \(x^4 + 4\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that \(x^4 + 4 = \left(x^2 + 2x + 2\right)\left(x^2 - 2x + 2\right)\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence solve the equation \(z^4 + 4 = 0\), for \(z \in \mathbb{C}\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Prove that \(n^4 + 4\) is not a prime number for any integer \(n \ge 2\).

idea: Write \(x^4 + 4 = \left(x^2 + 2\right)^2 - (2x)^2\), a difference of two squares. For part (c), a number that is a product of two whole numbers each greater than 1 is not prime.

solution.label: a
steps: \(\left(x^2 + 2\right)^2 - (2x)^2 = x^4 + 4x^2 + 4 - 4x^2 = x^4 + 4\), and a difference of squares factorises as \(\left(x^2 + 2 + 2x\right)\left(x^2 + 2 - 2x\right)\).

solution.label: c
steps: \(n^2 - 2n + 2 = (n - 1)^2 + 1 \ge 2\) for \(n \ge 2\), and \(n^2 + 2n + 2\) is larger still. So both factors are greater than 1, and \(n^4 + 4\) is not prime.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the value of \(\alpha + \beta + \gamma\) and the value of \(\alpha\beta\gamma\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the value of \(\alpha\beta + \beta\gamma + \gamma\alpha\).

idea: For \(ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d = 0\): the sum of the roots is \(-\frac{b}{a}\), the sum of the products in pairs is \(\frac{c}{a}\), and the product is \(-\frac{d}{a}\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the value of \(\alpha^2 + \beta^2\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find a quadratic equation, with integer coefficients, whose roots are \(\dfrac{\alpha}{\beta}\) and \(\dfrac{\beta}{\alpha}\).

idea: Write every symmetric expression in terms of \(\alpha + \beta\) and \(\alpha\beta\), which come straight from the coefficients. A quadratic with roots \(r\) and \(s\) is \(x^2 - (r + s)x + rs = 0\).

solution.label: b
steps: Sum of the new roots: \(\dfrac{\alpha}{\beta} + \dfrac{\beta}{\alpha} = \dfrac{\alpha^2 + \beta^2}{\alpha\beta} = \dfrac{9/4}{2} = \dfrac{9}{8}\). Product: \(\dfrac{\alpha}{\beta} \times \dfrac{\beta}{\alpha} = 1\).
\(x^2 - \dfrac{9}{8}x + 1 = 0\); multiply by 8. (The roots of the original equation are not real, since \(25 - 32 < 0\), but the method still works.)

stem: The equation \(x^3 - 6x^2 + 11x - 6 = 0\) has roots \(\alpha\), \(\beta\) and \(\gamma\). Without solving the equation, find the value of:

parts.label: a
parts.text: \(\alpha^2 + \beta^2 + \gamma^2\)

parts.label: b
parts.text: \(\dfrac{1}{\alpha} + \dfrac{1}{\beta} + \dfrac{1}{\gamma}\)

parts.label: c
parts.text: \(\alpha^2\beta^2 + \beta^2\gamma^2 + \gamma^2\alpha^2\)

idea: Let \(s_1 = \alpha + \beta + \gamma\), \(s_2 = \alpha\beta + \beta\gamma + \gamma\alpha\), \(s_3 = \alpha\beta\gamma\). Square a sum and subtract the cross terms: \(\left(\sum \alpha\right)^2 = \sum\alpha^2 + 2s_2\), and \(\left(\sum \alpha\beta\right)^2 = \sum\alpha^2\beta^2 + 2s_3s_1\).

stem: Consider the equation \(x^4 - 2x^3 + 3x^2 - 4x + 5 = 0\), with roots \(\alpha\), \(\beta\), \(\gamma\) and \(\delta\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the value of \(\alpha + \beta + \gamma + \delta\) and the value of the sum of the products of the roots taken two at a time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the value of \(\alpha^2 + \beta^2 + \gamma^2 + \delta^2\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence explain why the equation does not have four real roots.

idea: \(\left(\sum\alpha\right)^2 = \sum\alpha^2 + 2\sum\alpha\beta\). If every root were real, every square would be at least zero, so their sum could not be negative.

solution.label: a
steps: For \(x^4 + bx^3 + cx^2 + \cdots\) (leading coefficient 1): the sum of the roots is \(-b = 2\), and the sum of the pairwise products is \(c = 3\).

solution.label: c
steps: If all four roots were real, each \(\alpha^2 \ge 0\), so \(\sum\alpha^2 \ge 0\). But \(\sum\alpha^2 = -2 < 0\), so at least one root is not real (and non-real roots of a real polynomial come in conjugate pairs, so in fact at least two).
solution.answer: \(\sum\alpha^2 < 0\) is impossible for four real roots

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write \(f(x)\) in the form \(ax + b + \dfrac{c}{x + 1}\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write down the equations of the asymptotes of the graph of \(f\).

idea: Divide the numerator by \(x + 1\). As \(x \to \pm\infty\) the fraction \(\frac{c}{x + 1} \to 0\), so the graph approaches the line \(y = ax + b\): an oblique asymptote.

solution.label: b
steps: Vertical: where the denominator is zero, \(x = -1\) (the numerator is \(2 \ne 0\) there). Oblique: \(y = x + 2\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the equations of the vertical and horizontal asymptotes of the graph of \(f\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the points where the graph of \(f\) meets the axes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the \(x\)-coordinates of the points where the graph of \(f\) meets the line \(y = x\).

idea: Vertical asymptotes are at zeros of the denominator that are not zeros of the numerator. When the denominator has the higher degree, \(f(x) \to 0\) as \(x \to \pm\infty\).

solution.label: a
steps: \(x^2 - 4 = 0\) at \(x = \pm 2\); the numerator is not zero there. The degree of the denominator is greater than the degree of the numerator, so \(y = 0\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that \(f\) is an odd function.

parts.label: b
parts.text: By considering the equation \(f(x) = k\) as a quadratic in \(x\), find the range of \(f\).

idea: \(k\) is in the range exactly when \(f(x) = k\) has a real solution. Multiplying out gives a quadratic in \(x\), which has a real solution when its discriminant is at least zero.

solution.label: b
steps: If \(k = 0\), then \(x = 0\) works. If \(k \ne 0\), a real solution needs \(1 - 4k^2 \ge 0\), that is \(-\frac{1}{2} \le k \le \frac{1}{2}\).
So \(f\) takes every value from \(-\frac{1}{2}\) to \(\frac{1}{2}\): \(f(1) = \frac{1}{2}\) and \(f(-1) = -\frac{1}{2}\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that \(f(x) = x - 1 + \dfrac{4}{x - 1}\), and write down the equations of the asymptotes of the graph of \(f\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the range of \(f\).

idea: Let \(u = x - 1\), so \(f = u + \frac{4}{u}\). Then \(f(x) = k\) becomes a quadratic in \(u\), and a real solution needs a non-negative discriminant.

solution.label: a
steps: Vertical asymptote \(x = 1\); as \(x \to \pm\infty\), \(\frac{4}{x - 1} \to 0\), so the oblique asymptote is \(y = x - 1\).

solution.label: b
steps: A real solution needs \(k^2 - 16 \ge 0\), so \(k \le -4\) or \(k \ge 4\). (\(u = 0\) is never a solution, because the constant term is 4.)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the equation of the oblique asymptote of the graph of \(f\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the line \(y = m\) meets the graph of \(f\) where \(x^2 - mx + 2m + k = 0\), and hence show that the range of \(f\) is \(f(x) \le 4 - 2\sqrt{4 + k}\) or \(f(x) \ge 4 + 2\sqrt{4 + k}\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write down the range of \(f\) when \(k = 5\).

idea: Division gives the oblique asymptote. The line \(y = m\) meets the graph exactly when a quadratic in \(x\) has a real root, so the range is where its discriminant is non-negative.

solution.label: a
steps: \(x^2 + k = (x - 2)(x + 2) + 4 + k\), so \(f(x) = x + 2 + \dfrac{4 + k}{x - 2}\). As \(x \to \pm\infty\), the fraction tends to 0.

solution.label: b
steps: \(\dfrac{x^2 + k}{x - 2} = m\) gives \(x^2 + k = mx - 2m\), so \(x^2 - mx + 2m + k = 0\). (\(x = 2\) is never a root: it would give \(4 + k = 0\).)
Real roots need \(m^2 - 4(2m + k) \ge 0\), that is \(m^2 - 8m - 4k \ge 0\).
The roots of \(m^2 - 8m - 4k = 0\) are \(m = 4 \pm \sqrt{16 + 4k} = 4 \pm 2\sqrt{4 + k}\), and the quadratic in \(m\) is non-negative outside them.

stem: For each function below, determine whether it is odd, even, or neither. Justify each answer.
idea: Work out the function at \(-x\). Even means \(f(-x) = f(x)\) for every \(x\); odd means \(f(-x) = -f(x)\) for every \(x\). To show “neither”, one value of \(x\) that breaks both rules is enough.

solution.label: b
steps: \(g(-x) = x^2 + \cos(-x) = x^2 + \cos x = g(x)\), since cosine is even.

solution.label: c
steps: \(h(1) = 2\) and \(h(-1) = 0\). Since \(h(-1) \ne h(1)\) it is not even, and since \(h(-1) \ne -h(1)\) it is not odd.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that \((f \circ f)(x) = x\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence write down \(f^{-1}(x)\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the geometric property of the graph of \(f\) that this shows, and write down the range of \(f\).

idea: If applying \(f\) twice returns \(x\), then \(f\) undoes itself: \(f\) is its own inverse (self-inverse). The graph of an inverse is the reflection in \(y = x\), so a self-inverse graph is symmetric in that line.

solution.label: a
steps: Multiply the top and bottom by \(x - 3\): \(\dfrac{3(3x + 5) + 5(x - 3)}{3x + 5 - 3(x - 3)} = \dfrac{14x}{14} = x\).

solution.label: c
steps: The range of \(f\) is the domain of \(f^{-1} = f\). Also, \(f(x) = 3 + \frac{14}{x - 3}\) never equals 3.
solution.answer: The graph is symmetric in the line \(y = x\); range \(f(x) \ne 3\)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the least value of \(k\) for which \(f\) has an inverse function.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For this value of \(k\), find \(f^{-1}(x)\) and state its domain.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Solve the equation \(f(x) = f^{-1}(x)\).

idea: A function has an inverse only if it is one-to-one. Completing the square shows where the parabola turns; keep only one side of the vertex. Where an increasing function meets its inverse, the points lie on \(y = x\).

solution.label: a
steps: \(f(x) = (x - 3)^2 + 1\): the vertex is at \(x = 3\), and \(f\) is one-to-one on \(x \ge 3\) but not on any larger interval of this form.

solution.label: b
steps: The range of \(f\) is \(f(x) \ge 1\), which becomes the domain of \(f^{-1}\).

solution.label: c
steps: \(f\) is increasing on \(x \ge 3\), so the graphs of \(f\) and \(f^{-1}\) meet on \(y = x\): \(x^2 - 6x + 10 = x\), so \(x^2 - 7x + 10 = (x - 2)(x - 5) = 0\).
Only \(x = 5\) is in the domain \(x \ge 3\). Check: \(f(5) = 5\) and \(f^{-1}(5) = 3 + 2 = 5\).

stem: Let \(f\) be any function defined for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\). Define \(g(x) = \dfrac{f(x) + f(-x)}{2}\) and \(h(x) = \dfrac{f(x) - f(-x)}{2}\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that \(g\) is even and \(h\) is odd, and that \(f(x) = g(x) + h(x)\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find \(g\) and \(h\) when \(f(x) = e^x\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Prove that the only function that is both odd and even is \(f(x) = 0\), and hence explain why the functions \(g\) and \(h\) in part (a) are the only even and odd functions that add up to \(f\).

idea: Replace \(x\) with \(-x\) in the definitions and compare. For uniqueness, suppose \(f = g_1 + h_1 = g_2 + h_2\); then \(g_1 - g_2 = h_2 - h_1\) is both even and odd.

solution.label: a
steps: \(g(-x) = \dfrac{f(-x) + f(x)}{2} = g(x)\), so \(g\) is even. \(h(-x) = \dfrac{f(-x) - f(x)}{2} = -h(x)\), so \(h\) is odd.

solution.label: c
steps: If \(k\) is odd and even, then \(k(-x) = k(x)\) and \(k(-x) = -k(x)\), so \(k(x) = -k(x)\) and \(k(x) = 0\) for every \(x\).

If \(f = g_1 + h_1 = g_2 + h_2\) with \(g_1, g_2\) even and \(h_1, h_2\) odd, then \(g_1 - g_2 = h_2 - h_1\). The left side is even and the right side is odd, so both are 0: \(g_1 = g_2\) and \(h_1 = h_2\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that \(f\) is an odd function.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write \(f(x)\) without the modulus sign, using one formula for \(x \ge 0\) and one for \(x < 0\). Hence explain why \(f\) has an inverse.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find \(f^{-1}(x)\), using one formula for \(x \ge 0\) and one for \(x < 0\).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Solve the equation \(f(x) = f^{-1}(x)\).

idea: \(|x| = x\) when \(x \ge 0\) and \(|x| = -x\) when \(x < 0\). An increasing function is one-to-one, so it has an inverse; and an increasing function meets its inverse only on the line \(y = x\).

solution.label: b
steps: Both pieces are increasing, and they join at \((0, 0)\), so \(f\) is increasing on \(\mathbb{R}\), hence one-to-one, with range \(\mathbb{R}\).

solution.label: c
steps: For \(y \ge 0\): \(y = x^2\) with \(x \ge 0\), so \(x = \sqrt{y}\). For \(y < 0\): \(y = -x^2\) with \(x < 0\), so \(x = -\sqrt{-y}\).

solution.label: d
steps: \(f\) is increasing, so the solutions are where \(f(x) = x\): \(x\,|x| = x\), so \(x = 0\) or \(|x| = 1\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sketch the graph of \(y = |f(x)|\), showing the coordinates of the points where it meets the axes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: On the same axes, sketch the graph of \(y = f(|x|)\), showing the coordinates of the points where it meets the axes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write down the range of \(y = f(|x|)\).

idea: \(|f(x)|\) reflects the parts of the graph below the \(x\)-axis up into it. \(f(|x|)\) keeps the part of the graph for \(x \ge 0\) and reflects it in the \(y\)-axis.

solution.label: a
steps: \(y = 2x - 4\) is below the axis for \(x < 2\); reflect that part up. Vertex \((2, 0)\), \(y\)-intercept \(|-4| = 4\).

solution.label: b
steps: For \(x \ge 0\), \(f(|x|) = 2x - 4\); reflect this in the \(y\)-axis. Vertex \((0, -4)\), \(x\)-intercepts \((\pm 2, 0)\).
solution.answer: V shape with vertex \((0, -4)\), through \((-2, 0)\) and \((2, 0)\)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write \(f(x)\) in factorised form, and in the form \((x - h)^2 + k\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Sketch the graph of \(y = \dfrac{1}{f(x)}\). Show the equations of the asymptotes, the \(y\)-intercept, and the coordinates of the local maximum point.

idea: Zeros of \(f\) become vertical asymptotes of \(\frac{1}{f}\). Where \(f\) is large, \(\frac{1}{f}\) is close to 0. A minimum of \(f\) at a negative value becomes a maximum of \(\frac{1}{f}\), and the sign of \(\frac{1}{f}\) is the sign of \(f\).

solution.label: b
steps: Vertical asymptotes at the zeros of \(f\): \(x = -1\) and \(x = 3\). As \(x \to \pm\infty\), \(f(x) \to \infty\), so \(\frac{1}{f(x)} \to 0\): horizontal asymptote \(y = 0\).
\(f\) has its minimum \(-4\) at \(x = 1\), so \(\frac{1}{f}\) has a local maximum \(-\frac{1}{4}\) there. \(y\)-intercept: \(\frac{1}{f(0)} = -\frac{1}{3}\).
\(\frac{1}{f}\) is positive outside the asymptotes and negative between them.

stem: Let \(f(x) = x^3 - 4x\), for \(x \in \mathbb{R}\). The graph of \(f\) has a local maximum at \(\left(-\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}, \dfrac{16}{3\sqrt{3}}\right)\) and a local minimum at \(\left(\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}, -\dfrac{16}{3\sqrt{3}}\right)\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of solutions of the equation \(|f(x)| = 2\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of solutions of the equation \(f(|x|) = -1\), and find the solutions.

idea: \(|f(x)| = 2\) means \(f(x) = 2\) or \(f(x) = -2\); compare 2 with the local maximum value \(\frac{16}{3\sqrt{3}} = 3.07\ldots\). \(f(|x|) = -1\) uses only the part of the graph with \(x \ge 0\), then reflects it: each positive solution gives two solutions.

solution.label: a
steps: \(\frac{16}{3\sqrt{3}} = 3.079\ldots > 2\), so the line \(y = 2\) meets the cubic three times, and by symmetry (\(f\) is odd) so does \(y = -2\). The six points are different.

solution.label: b
steps: For \(x \ge 0\), solve \(x^3 - 4x = -1\), that is \(x^3 - 4x + 1 = 0\). With a GDC its roots are \(-2.114\ldots\), \(0.2541\ldots\) and \(1.860\ldots\); two are positive.

stem: The graph of \(y = f(x)\) has a local maximum at \((2, 5)\), a horizontal asymptote \(y = 1\), and passes through \((-2, 0)\). Let \(g(x) = 3f(2x - 4) - 1\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the local maximum of the graph of \(g\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write down the equation of the horizontal asymptote of the graph of \(g\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the point on the graph of \(g\) that corresponds to \((-2, 0)\).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe a sequence of transformations that maps the graph of \(f\) onto the graph of \(g\).

idea: A point \((a, b)\) on \(y = f(x)\) corresponds to the point of \(y = 3f(2x - 4) - 1\) with \(2x - 4 = a\) and \(y = 3b - 1\): solve for \(x\), then transform the height.

solution.label: d
steps: \(f(2x - 4) = f\left(2(x - 2)\right)\): a horizontal stretch by scale factor \(\frac{1}{2}\), then a translation 2 units right. Then a vertical stretch by scale factor 3, then a translation 1 unit down.
solution.answer: Horizontal stretch \(\times\frac{1}{2}\); translate 2 right; vertical stretch \(\times 3\); translate 1 down

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the coordinates of the points where the graph of \(f\) meets the axes. Given that \(f'(x) = 3x(x - 2)\), find the coordinates of the stationary points of \(f\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Sketch the graph of \(y = f(|x|)\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the set of values of \(k\) for which the equation \(f(|x|) = k\) has exactly four solutions.

idea: \(f(|x|)\) uses only the graph for \(x \ge 0\), mirrored in the \(y\)-axis. So count solutions with \(x > 0\) and double them, then add 1 if \(x = 0\) is a solution.

solution.label: a
steps: \(f'(x) = 0\) at \(x = 0\) and \(x = 2\): \(f(0) = 4\), \(f(2) = 0\). The cubic has positive leading coefficient, so \((0, 4)\) is a local maximum and \((2, 0)\) a local minimum.

solution.label: b
steps: For \(x \ge 0\) the graph falls from \((0, 4)\) to \((2, 0)\) and then rises. Reflect this part in the \(y\)-axis.
solution.answer: Symmetric W-like shape: maximum \((0, 4)\), touching the axis at \((\pm 2, 0)\)

solution.label: c
steps: For \(x > 0\): if \(0 < k < 4\), \(f(x) = k\) has one solution in \(0 < x < 2\) and one in \(x > 2\), so \(f(|x|) = k\) has four.

\(k = 4\): \(f(x) = 4\) gives \(x^2(x - 3) = 0\), so \(x = 0\) or \(x = 3\): solutions \(0, \pm 3\), three in all. \(k = 0\): \(x = \pm 2\), two. \(k > 4\): one positive solution, so two. \(k < 0\): none.

idea: Split into the two cases \(2x - 3 = 4 - x\) and \(2x - 3 = -(4 - x)\). A modulus is never negative, so check each answer in the original equation: \(4 - x\) must not be negative.
Both sides are non-negative, so squaring keeps the inequality the right way round: \(|a| > |b| \iff a^2 > b^2\). Then solve a quadratic inequality.

steps: Check: \(x = 3\) gives \(4 > 2\); \(x = 0\) gives \(1 > 4\), which is false.

idea: Collect everything on one side, find where the cubic is zero with a GDC, then use the shape of the graph (positive leading coefficient) to decide where it is positive.

steps: \(x^3 + x^2 - 2x - 1 > 0\). With a GDC the roots are \(-1.801\ldots\), \(-0.4450\ldots\) and \(1.246\ldots\)
A cubic with positive leading coefficient is positive between the first two roots and after the third.

stem: This question is about the inequality \(\dfrac{x + 3}{x - 1} \le 2\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the inequality \(\dfrac{x + 3}{x - 1} \le 2\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence solve the inequality \(\dfrac{|x| + 3}{|x| - 1} \le 2\).

idea: Do not multiply by \(x - 1\), whose sign is unknown. Move everything to one side and write it as a single fraction, then use a sign table. In part (b) replace \(x\) by \(|x|\) in the answer to part (a).

solution.label: a
steps: The fraction is zero at \(x = 5\) and undefined at \(x = 1\). For \(x < 1\): top positive, bottom negative, so negative. For \(1 < x < 5\): positive. For \(x > 5\): negative.

solution.label: b
steps: By part (a) with \(|x|\) in place of \(x\): \(|x| < 1\) or \(|x| \ge 5\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write \(g(x)\) without modulus signs on each of the intervals \(x < 1\), \(1 \le x \le 5\) and \(x > 5\), and sketch the graph of \(g\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Solve the equation \(g(x) = 6\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the set of values of \(k\) for which the equation \(g(x) = k\) has exactly two solutions, and the value of \(k\) for which it has infinitely many.

idea: Each modulus changes formula where its inside is zero, at \(x = 1\) and \(x = 5\). On each interval \(g\) is a straight line, so the graph is made of three line segments.

solution.label: b
steps: \(6 - 2x = 6\) gives \(x = 0\) (which is \(< 1\)). \(2x - 6 = 6\) gives \(x = 6\) (which is \(> 5\)). The middle piece is 4, never 6.

solution.label: c
steps: The least value of \(g\) is 4, taken at every point of \(1 \le x \le 5\). A line \(y = k\) with \(k > 4\) meets each sloping piece once; \(k < 4\) misses the graph.
solution.answer: Exactly two solutions for \(k > 4\); infinitely many for \(k = 4\)
